newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russians form group to fight video piracy.
newsitem.headline: Russians form group to fight video piracy.

text.p: A group of Russian film distributors and television companies have formed an association to fight rampant video piracy, officials said on Monday.
"In Russia, the video piracy situation is very bad, which means it's a great place to be a video pirate," said Grigory Simanovich, a spokesman for Russian Public Television ORT.
"Russia has taken virtually no steps against video piracy, and as a result the government loses $250 million a year in tax revenues," he said.

The new Russian Anti-Pirate Organisation includes ORT, Mosfilm, the country's leading studio, official video distributors, the U.S. Motion Picture Association and others in the fight against the sale of unauthorised videos.
The group planned to work out a concrete plan of action in the near future, Simanovich said.

Russians sell pirated videos in street kiosks and large outdoor markets across the country, often for as little as a few dollars a film. Many movies appear on pirated video soon after their premieres in the United States.
Earlier this year, the International Intellectual Property Alliance asked U.S. trade officials to consider sanctions against Russia if Moscow failed to improve copyright protection.

The group, which represents software and entertainment companies, said 70 to 90 percent of the Russian market in goods such as videos, music and computer software CDs came from pirated sales, causing companies an annual loss of $1 billion.

The International Federation of the Phonograph Industry, which represents recording companies, has also asked the European Union to ban Russia from the World Trade Organisation unless it deals with the problem.
Russian police make occasional raids against vendors of illegal videos and CDs, but make few arrests. Few sellers are intimidated enough to find another line of work.
Russian video piracy partly has its roots in the Soviet era, when film lovers passed around bootleg copies of Western films forbidden by the government.
